claims.text: High-entropy alloys comprise five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and can form a single crystalline solid-solution phase.
The initial nanoparticles have homogeneous, well-mixed surface atoms.
The structural and chemical stability of equimolar multi-metal nanoparticles is governed by a temperature-dependent balance between configurational entropy and surface-ordering enthalpy.
High configurational entropy favors the single solid-solution phase over intermetallic formation or phase segregation.
At higher temperatures, configurational entropy maintains a well-mixed nanoparticle surface.
HEA nanoparticles can retain structurally similar, well-mixed configurations from 573 to 1000 K.
Enthalpic interactions can favor intermetallic ordering or phase separation rather than a homogeneous high-entropy state.
At the lower end of the operating range, ordering enthalpy may overcome entropy and cause localized surface ordering or segregation.
Surface ordering or segregation compromises the overall structural and chemical stability of the nanoparticles.
Surface reorganization affects catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Nanoparticles that preserve well-mixed surfaces will exhibit consistent catalytic and thermoelectric behavior throughout 473–1923 K.
The onset of surface segregation or ordering will correlate with degraded catalytic or thermoelectric performance relative to the initial baseline.
The room-temperature baseline has no observable surface segregation.
The proposed entropy–enthalpy mechanism applies across the full temperature range of 473–1923 K.
Significantly non-equimolar compositions may shift the entropy–enthalpy balance and invalidate the prediction.
The transition temperature and kinetics of surface segregation are uncertain.
A lack of correlation between surface mixing changes and performance changes across 473–1923 K would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says that preserved well-mixed surfaces should produce consistent performance, but the falsification rule also treats a well-mixed surface at all temperatures with no performance differences as falsifying. That observation is compatible with the stated prediction rather than decisively contradictory to it.
